standard_prerequisites.name: n-types and their preservation under equivalence
standard_prerequisites.statement: If X is equivalent to an n-type then X is an n-type.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is applied at source line 159 to replace the path space of the sigma type by an equivalent sigma type.

standard_prerequisites.name: Paths in a sigma type
standard_prerequisites.statement: (a_1,b_1) = (a_2,b_2) is equivalent to Sigma p : a_1 = a_2, trans p b_1 = b_2.
standard_prerequisites.use: It produces the equivalence displayed at source line 158 that the induction step works with.

standard_prerequisites.name: The induction hypothesis on n-types
standard_prerequisites.statement: Contractible types and their path spaces behave as in the definition of the hierarchy.
standard_prerequisites.use: The base case at lines 148-151 and the step at lines 153-161 are both reduced to the inductive hypothesis.

core_obligations: Base case n = -2: for A contractible with centre a_0 and B(a_0) contractible with centre b_0, show that (a_0,b_0) is a centre for Sigma x:A B(x), comparing an arbitrary (a,b) with it componentwise (source lines 148-151).
Induction step: assume A is an (n+1)-type and each B(a) is an (n+1)-type, fix (a_1,b_1) and (a_2,b_2), and show that their path space is an n-type (source lines 153-156).
Rewrite that path space by the equivalence Sigma p : a_1 = a_2, trans p b_1 = b_2 (source lines 157-158) and replace it by an equivalent type using preservation under equivalence (source line 159).
Discharge the resulting goal by the inductive hypothesis, since a_1 = a_2 is an n-type and so is the fiber of the transport (source lines 160-161).

proof_roadmap.step: Set up the induction on n.
Base case: build the centre of the sigma type componentwise.
Induction step: fix two elements and reduce to their path space.
Use the sigma path equivalence and closure under equivalence to reach the inductive hypothesis.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is Theorem 7.1.8 at source lines 140-143: if A is an n-type and every B(a) is an n-type then Sigma x:A B(x) is an n-type. The proof (source lines 145-162) handles the two ends of the hierarchy separately and neither is a one-liner: the base case at lines 148-151 builds the centre of contraction of the sigma type componentwise, while the induction step at lines 153-161 first has to replace the path space of the sigma type by the equivalent type Sigma p : a_1 = a_2, trans p b_1 = b_2 using the sigma path theorem (line 158), then invoke preservation of n-types under equivalence (line 159) before the inductive hypothesis applies. The statement gives no hint that the transport of b_1 along p is what has to be shown truncated.
